soil-env-109.title: How organic carbon keeps a soil working
soil-env-109.text: In one study of sandy soils, organic carbon accounted for up to 76% of the variation in cation exchange capacity, the soil's power to hold nutrient ions. That is one of many services organic carbon sustains. Together they add up to soil health, a soil's capacity to provide services. Carbon benchmarks used to judge it include CO2 release, humus levels and microbial metabolic activity. In sandy soils, bulk density falls as organic carbon rises, and bulk density is needed to calculate carbon stocks. Organic carbon also rises with silt and clay content and is highest in the clay fraction, where fine particles bind decomposing matter into protective aggregates.

soil-env-103.title: Two speeds of the carbon cycle
soil-env-103.text: Some carbon turns over in years; some takes millions. The carbon cycle splits into a fast biological cycle and a slow geological one. The fast cycle runs through living things, moving carbon between the atmosphere, land and marine ecosystems, soils and seafloor sediments. It includes annual cycles driven by photosynthesis and decadal cycles of vegetation growth and decomposition. The slow cycle runs through rocks. Weathering returns carbon to the atmosphere by degassing and to the ocean by rivers, over spans of millions of years. Between 10 and 100 million tonnes of carbon move around it in a given year.

soil-env-114.title: When warming soils breathe out more carbon
soil-env-114.text: A warming experiment at Harvard, run since 1991, suggests the top metre of soils could release about 190 petagrams of carbon by 2100. That release is the soil carbon feedback: carbon leaving soils in response to global warming, which in turn adds to the warming. Soils hold roughly two to three times as much carbon as the atmosphere, so the feedback is crucial for future climate. Faster soil respiration is the main cause. Measurements imply that 4 °C of warming raises annual soil respiration by up to 37%. Between 1989 and 2008, global soil respiration rose by about 0.1% a year, most likely because warming sped up the decomposition of soil organic matter. A 2018 study found climate-driven soil carbon losses already occurring across many ecosystems, with a detectable global trend. Observations of thawing permafrost suggest a linear, chronic release of greenhouse gases as warming continues. Gaps remain. Global decomposition models poorly represent soil animals such as insects and worms, and their interactions with microbes.

soil-env-117.title: Carbon pools, the Earth's carbon reservoirs
soil-env-117.text: The atmosphere, the oceans, soil, plants and fossil fuels share one label: each is a carbon pool. A carbon pool is any reservoir in the Earth system where carbon resides in some chemical form for a period of time. It is the overarching term, and a carbon sink is one type of pool. The two words mean slightly different things, and both matter for understanding the carbon cycle. Related terms are reservoir, sequestration, source and uptake.

soil-env-104.title: Carbon on land, above and below ground
soil-env-104.text: About 500 gigatons of carbon sit above ground in plants and other organisms, while soil holds approximately 1,500 gigatons. Together they make up the terrestrial carbon pool: the carbon held in all living and dead land organisms and in soils. Most land carbon is organic, but about a third of soil carbon is inorganic, in forms such as calcium carbonate. Because land uptake depends on living things, it follows daily and seasonal cycles. Those rhythms show up in the Keeling curve of CO2 measurements. Carbon leaves the land pool by burning or respiration, or by export to the ocean in rivers. Some stays sequestered in soils as inert carbon, for up to thousands of years, until erosion washes it into rivers or soil respiration releases it. How long soil holds carbon depends on local climate, so it changes as the climate changes.

soil-env-105.title: Clearing forests, releasing carbon
soil-env-105.text: Replace a forest with cropland or a town, and carbon once stored on land ends up in the atmosphere. Cropland and urban land store comparatively little carbon. That release, chiefly from turning forest into farmland or towns, is the carbon cost of land-use change. Since the invention of agriculture, people have shifted the carbon cycle over centuries by changing the mix of vegetation on land. The change has also cut biodiversity, lowering ecosystems' resilience and their ability to remove carbon from the air. Reforestation, deliberate or natural, can reverse the effect.

soil-env-213.title: Feedbacks that speed up or slow down warming
soil-env-213.text: The IPCC estimates that permafrost could release the equivalent of 14-175 billion tonnes of CO2 per 1 °C of warming. Releases like that are climate change feedbacks: natural processes that change how much the planet warms for a given amount of greenhouse gas emissions. Positive feedbacks amplify warming, and negative ones damp it. The labels do not mean good or bad. Physical feedbacks include less reflective snow and ice and more water vapour. Biological ones mostly involve how fast plants take up CO2. The carbon cycle absorbs more than half of yearly CO2 emissions into plants and the ocean. That share will fall as sinks saturate and drought and wildfire increase. Methane from land, especially wetlands, and nitrous oxide from land and oceans are a known positive feedback. The sum of all feedbacks is negative but becoming less so, so warming will accelerate if emissions continue at current levels. The carbon side remains uncertain, and permafrost thaw releases CO2 and methane in ways that are hard to model.

soil-env-131.title: Frozen ground on the high mountains
soil-env-131.text: In 2009 permafrost was found on Mount Kilimanjaro. Alpine permafrost is permafrost at high elevations, in mountains cold enough to keep the ground frozen year after year. Extensive alpine permafrost generally needs a mean annual air temperature of −3 °C, though some mountains hold it at −1 °C. It is hard to study, and systematic research began only in the 1970s. Regional estimates collected in 2014 put its global extent at 3,560,000 km2. The Qinghai-Tibet Plateau holds the largest area, 1,300,000 km2. The frozen layer can even lie beneath warmer soil that supports vegetation.

soil-env-138.title: Building on frozen ground without thawing it
soil-env-138.text: Norilsk and Yakutsk, both in Russia, are the only two large cities built on continuous permafrost. Their engineers face one central danger. Heat from a building or pipeline can thaw the soil, and as ice turns to water the ground loses its ability to support the structure. Construction on permafrost therefore keeps the ground frozen. Wood pile foundations, pioneered by Mikhail Kim in Norilsk, should reach 15 metres, where the temperature stays at about −5 °C all year. Other methods are gravel pads 1–2 m thick and ammonia heat pipes, as in the supports of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline.

soil-env-145.title: From a blocked well in Yakutsk to a world science
soil-env-145.text: In 1684 frozen ground stopped well digging in Yakutsk, one of the earliest reports of permafrost. Until the mid-20th century most of the literature on it was in Russian. Karl Ernst von Baer, often called the founder of scientific permafrost research, published from 1838 and wrote the first permafrost textbook in 1843. The English word arrived in 1943. Siemon William Muller coined it from permanently frozen ground, translating the Russian vechnaia merzlota. The First International Conference on Permafrost met at Purdue University in November 1963, and the International Permafrost Association was created in 1983.

soil-env-135.title: Massive ground ice, frozen soil that is mostly ice
soil-env-135.text: In massive ground ice, the ice exceeds 250 percent of the dry soil by mass. Its beds are at least 2 m thick and 10 m across, ranging from icy mud to pure ice. Of the four kinds of ground ice, only buried surface ice and intrasedimental ice, which grows within the sediment, get large enough to count as massive. Pore ice and ice wedges do not. Segregational ice, the main intrasedimental type, forms as water migrates to the freezing front, mostly in silts of low salinity. In the top 2.5 m, forming it takes 1–1000 years in clay, 10–10,000 years in peat and 1,000–1,000,000 years in silt.

soil-env-152.title: Yedoma, Ice Age permafrost packed with carbon
soil-env-152.text: Yedoma covers more than one million square kilometers from northeast Siberia to Alaska and Canada, in many places tens of meters thick. It is ice-rich, organic-rich permafrost of Pleistocene age, about 2% carbon by mass and 50–90% ice by volume. It forms in poorly drained, severely cold lowlands with ice wedge polygons, sparse vegetation, intense periglacial weathering and nearby sources of sediment. Yedoma may hold about 210 to 500 Gt of carbon, a multiple of yearly fossil fuel emissions. As it thaws it becomes a significant methane source, about 4 Tg of CH4 a year. It has done this before. At the end of the last ice age, thawing yedoma and its thaw lakes may have caused 33 to 87% of the high-latitude rise in atmospheric methane.

soil-env-133.title: When permafrost reached Hungary
soil-env-133.text: During the Last Glacial Maximum, continuous permafrost covered all of ice-free Europe south to about Szeged in Hungary. In East Asia it reached as far south as present-day Changchun. North America had only a narrow belt south of the ice sheet, but in the drier west it stretched to the southern borders of Idaho and Oregon. The Southern Hemisphere also shows evidence of former, probably discontinuous permafrost, in central Otago and Argentine Patagonia.

soil-env-134.title: How deep permafrost goes, and how slowly
soil-env-134.text: In the northern Lena and Yana River basins of Siberia, permafrost runs 1,493 m deep. Its bottom, the permafrost base, lies where Earth's geothermal heat balances the mean surface temperature at 0 °C. Base depth ranges from less than a meter to that Siberian extreme. Growth slows sharply after the first few metres. At Prudhoe Bay, Alaska, permafrost reaches 4.44 m after 1 year but 687.7 m only after 775,000 years. That deep layer took over half a million years to form, spanning several Pleistocene glacial cycles. Permafrost in soil conducts heat less well than permafrost in bedrock, so the geothermal gradient affects it less.

soil-env-137.title: Life above and within permanently frozen ground
soil-env-137.text: Even frozen, permafrost soil typically holds from 1 to 1000 million microorganisms per gram. Permafrost ecology is how permanently frozen ground shapes the plants, animals and microbes that live with it. Only shallow-rooted plants survive over permafrost. Black spruce tolerates limited rooting zones and dominates where permafrost is extensive. Most permafrost bacteria and fungi cannot be cultured in the lab, so scientists identify them by DNA-based techniques. The living ones show adaptations to sub-zero conditions, including reduced metabolism and anaerobic metabolism, which runs without oxygen.

soil-env-136.title: Polygons, slumps and mounds: the shapes of frozen ground
soil-env-136.text: Frozen ground sculpts its own surface. Permafrost landforms are the features built as that ground freezes, cracks and thaws. Thermal contraction cracks that become ice wedges, together with solifluction downslope, create polygons, rings, steps and other patterned ground. Melting ground ice in ice-rich permafrost starts the collapse features described in {{ref:soil-env-153}}: lakes, thaw slumps, thermal-erosion gullies and active layer detachments. In Arctic bogs, meltwater trapped over deep permafrost freezes into ice lenses that push the ground up into mounds. These grow into palsas, peat mounds 15–150 m long but under 6 m tall, and larger pingos, 3–70 m high and up to 1,000 m across.

soil-env-142.title: Thawing ground under Arctic towns and roads
soil-env-142.text: As of 2021, 1162 settlements with about 5 million people sit on Arctic permafrost. Beneath 42% of them, the permafrost is expected to thaw by 2050. That threat reaches settlements, roads, pipelines and buildings alike. By 2050 nearly 70% of infrastructure in permafrost areas could be at high risk, including 30–50% of critical infrastructure, at costs of tens of billions of dollars. In Alaska alone, damages by 2100 would reach $4.6 billion under the high-emission RCP8.5 scenario. The Qinghai–Tibet Plateau is warming at twice the global rate. Already 40% of its permafrost is warm, and around 30% of its roads are damaged.

soil-env-143.title: Toxic waste and mercury waiting in the ice
soil-env-143.text: An estimated 800,000 tons of mercury lie frozen in permafrost soil. For much of the 20th century, permafrost was thought to preserve buried material indefinitely, so it became a popular site for hazardous waste disposal. About 4500 industrial facilities handle hazardous chemicals in Arctic permafrost areas. Some 13,000 to 20,000 heavily contaminated sites, 70% of them in Russia, are trapped in the frozen ground. Thaw could release them. After thaw, around 70% of the mercury is taken up by vegetation. Under the high-emission RCP8.5 scenario, enough would reach the Yukon River basin by 2050 to make its fish unsafe to eat under EPA guidelines.
